title: A coating that lets concrete repair its own cracks
key_problem: Small cracks let water and salt reach the steel inside concrete. Finding and sealing them by hand is slow and expensive, so most are fixed only once the damage is visible.
plain_explanation: We developed a spray-on coating that contains dormant bacteria and a mineral food source. When a crack opens and water gets in, the bacteria wake up and produce limestone that fills the crack. The coating is applied once, like paint, on new or existing structures. In our tests it sealed cracks up to 0.6 mm wide within four weeks, with no human intervention.
concrete_examples: Extend the life of motorway bridges and parking decks exposed to de-icing salt
Reduce inspection rounds on water tanks and tunnels
Offer a premium 'self-maintaining' finish on precast concrete elements
case_studies: Bacteria-based healing agents mixed into fresh concrete have been commercialised in the Netherlands since 2017. Our approach differs because it is a surface coating, so it also works on the existing building stock.
feasibility: The coating works reliably in the lab and on two outdoor test walls in Milan. The open questions are shelf life of the spray (currently three months) and performance below 5 degrees Celsius. Both need about a year of engineering with an industrial partner.
market_problem: Infrastructure owners in Europe spend billions each year on concrete repair, mostly reactive. There is no low-cost preventive product that works on structures already in service.
draft_business_plan: License the formulation to an established construction-chemicals producer, with a royalty per litre sold. Keep the right to run a small spin-off for specialised applications such as heritage buildings.
go_to_market: Start with one pilot on a public parking structure, publish the inspection data after 12 months, then approach motorway operators with the evidence.

title: A battery separator that can be recycled with the cells
key_problem: The thin plastic film that separates the two sides of a lithium battery cannot be recovered today. It is burnt during recycling and limits how clean the recovered metals are.
plain_explanation: We made a separator from a cellulose-based material that dissolves in a mild water solution at the end of the battery's life. This makes the rest of the cell easier to take apart and the recovered metals purer. In the lab, cells using our separator charge and discharge as well as standard ones for 500 cycles.
concrete_examples: Simplify recycling lines for electric-vehicle batteries
Help cell makers meet the recycled-content targets of the EU Battery Regulation
Replace fossil-based plastics in stationary storage batteries
case_studies: Paper-based separators were used in early capacitors and are being revisited by several Nordic pulp companies. None so far has been designed for end-of-life recovery.
feasibility: Proven on coin cells only. Scaling to pouch cells is the next step and requires access to a pilot coating line. Honest estimate: two to three years before a cell maker could qualify it.
market_problem: Battery recyclers lose value because separators contaminate the black mass. Cell makers face rising recycled-content obligations with no easy lever on the separator.
draft_business_plan: Create a spin-off that produces separator film under licence from the university, first for stationary storage where qualification is shorter.
go_to_market: Joint development with one recycler and one cell maker, funded partly by an EU Battery Partnership call.

title: Hearing when a wind turbine is about to break
key_problem: Gearbox failures stop wind turbines for weeks. Current monitoring uses vibration sensors that detect problems late and cost a lot to install.
plain_explanation: We place a cheap microphone at the bottom of the tower and let software listen to the turbine. The software has learned what a healthy gearbox sounds like and flags small changes weeks before a failure. It runs on a small computer inside the tower and sends a simple alert to the operator.
concrete_examples: Plan gearbox repairs in summer instead of after a winter breakdown
Retrofit older turbines that have no vibration sensors
Prioritise inspection crews across a large wind park
case_studies: Acoustic monitoring is standard for detecting leaks in pipelines. A Danish operator tested an early version of our system on 12 turbines in 2025 and caught two gearbox faults in advance.
feasibility: Tested for eight months on a real wind park. Works well on onshore turbines; offshore noise conditions are untested. The software is ready, the hardware needs certification.
market_problem: Wind operators lose revenue on every unplanned stop and pay premium prices for emergency repairs. Monitoring that is cheap enough for older turbines does not exist.
draft_business_plan: Software subscription per turbine per year, with the microphone kit sold at cost.
go_to_market: Extend the pilot to a full park with one Nordic operator, then sell through turbine service companies.

title: A 15-minute bedside test for sepsis
key_problem: Sepsis kills when it is recognised too late. Today's lab tests take hours, and doctors often start antibiotics without being sure.
plain_explanation: We identified a combination of three molecules in the blood that rises early in sepsis. We built a small cartridge, similar to a glucose test, that measures them from a drop of blood in 15 minutes. In a study on 240 emergency patients, it identified sepsis earlier than the standard test.
concrete_examples: Triage patients in emergency departments within minutes
Avoid unnecessary antibiotics and the resistance they create
Monitor high-risk patients after surgery
case_studies: Rapid bedside tests for heart attacks changed emergency care in the 2000s. Our test follows the same model for sepsis.
feasibility: Clinical data is strong but from one hospital. A multi-centre study and the CE marking under the EU medical device regulation are needed, which takes two to three years and significant funding.
market_problem: Hospitals lack a fast, reliable sepsis test. The cost of late treatment is high in lives and in intensive-care days.
draft_business_plan: License to a diagnostics company that already sells point-of-care readers, so the cartridge plugs into an installed base.
go_to_market: Partner with a diagnostics company for the multi-centre study; the partner handles CE marking and distribution.

title: Turning cheese whey into dairy protein without cows
key_problem: Cheese makers produce large volumes of whey that are expensive to treat. At the same time, demand for animal-free dairy proteins is growing.
plain_explanation: We are designing a yeast that feeds on whey sugar and produces milk protein. The idea is to use a waste stream as the food source instead of refined sugar. So far we have shown on paper and in small flasks that the yeast can grow on whey; protein yield is still low.
concrete_examples: Give cheese plants a new revenue line from their whey
Supply protein for plant-based cheese that melts like real cheese
Lower the cost of precision-fermentation protein
case_studies: Several US start-ups produce milk proteins by fermentation from sugar. Using whey as feedstock has not been done at scale.
feasibility: Early stage. The yield must improve roughly tenfold before the economics make sense. This is a two to four year research effort.
market_problem: Dairy processors lack profitable outlets for whey; precision-fermentation companies pay a lot for sugar feedstock.
draft_business_plan: Research contract with a dairy cooperative first, then a joint venture if yields reach target.
go_to_market: Too early. First objective is a funded research partnership.

title: On-demand buses that make rural transport affordable
key_problem: Fixed bus lines in rural areas run mostly empty. Cutting them leaves people without a car isolated.
plain_explanation: Our software plans minibus routes every few minutes based on the trips people book by phone or app. It groups passengers going in the same direction and picks the shortest detours. In a six-month trial around a small French town, it carried the same passengers with 40% fewer kilometres driven.
concrete_examples: Replace half-empty rural bus lines with demand-responsive service
Coordinate school, medical and leisure trips in one fleet
Plan night services in suburbs
case_studies: Demand-responsive transport exists in Finland and Germany, often with high costs per trip. Our routing method was benchmarked against two commercial tools and needed fewer vehicles.
feasibility: Already working in a real trial. The method is published. What is missing is a production-grade product team and an operator to deploy it in a second region.
market_problem: Local authorities must keep rural mobility running on shrinking budgets and look for cheaper alternatives to fixed lines.
draft_business_plan: Software-as-a-service sold to transport operators and local authorities, priced per vehicle.
go_to_market: Answer public tenders together with an established bus operator.

title: A low-cost sensor that counts microplastics in wastewater
key_problem: New EU rules require treatment plants to monitor microplastics, but today's method needs a lab and several days per sample.
plain_explanation: We built a flow cell that shines light through the water and recognises plastic particles by the way they scatter it. It gives a count every few minutes instead of every few days. The lab prototype agrees well with reference measurements on clean samples; real wastewater is still a challenge.
concrete_examples: Continuous monitoring at treatment plant outlets
Check the efficiency of filters installed against microplastics
Screen industrial discharge from textile or plastics plants
case_studies: Optical particle counters are standard in drinking-water plants for other particles. Adapting them to plastics is new.
feasibility: Works on clean water in the lab. Fouling by organic matter in real wastewater is the main risk and needs field tests at a treatment plant.
market_problem: Water utilities face a new monitoring obligation with no affordable continuous method.
draft_business_plan: Sell sensors and a monitoring service to water utilities, possibly through an instrument manufacturer.
go_to_market: Field test with one utility, then partner with an instrument maker for distribution.

title: Robots that sort used clothing by fibre type
key_problem: Only a small share of used textiles is recycled into new fibre, because sorting by material is done by hand and is too slow.
plain_explanation: Our robot cell looks at each garment with a special camera that recognises cotton, polyester and blends, then picks it into the right bin. It handles about one garment per second, ten times faster than manual sorting. The cell has run for a year at a sorting centre near Karlsruhe.
concrete_examples: Automate sorting at textile collection centres
Supply pure fibre streams to chemical recyclers
Help brands meet upcoming textile take-back obligations
case_studies: Optical sorting transformed plastic packaging recycling. Two Nordic pilots use similar cameras for textiles but sort manually afterwards.
feasibility: Ready for industrial deployment. The remaining work is building cells in series and setting up maintenance.
market_problem: Textile sorters cannot process the volumes created by mandatory separate collection from 2025 onwards.
draft_business_plan: Sell or lease robot cells to sorting centres with a service contract.
go_to_market: First series of five cells with the current pilot partner, then expansion through a recycling equipment distributor.
